title: How to Read a VC Fund Announcement Before You Pitch
summary: How to Read a VC Fund Announcement Before You Pitch
body_markdown:
Founders sometimes find a fund announcement and read it as ‘this firm has money for companies like mine.’ There are three separate claims in that sentence. The vehicle might have raised money. It might be making new investments. It might even invest in your kind of company. A good list tests all three instead of letting one press release stand in for the rest.


## Find the vehicle


Daybreak announced $100 million across two vehicles: $75 million for its second core fund and $25 million for a separate opportunistic vehicle. Haystack announced an $85 million core fund and a $25 million companion. Those aren’t two examples of a firm writing checks from the whole headline number. If you’re building a list of smaller early-stage funds, record the vehicle and its purpose in separate columns. A small number attached to a follow-on vehicle can make a terrible lead.


Do the same with the amount. A target is what fund managers hope to raise. A first close is an amount committed at a particular point, not necessarily the intended final total. A firm’s assets under management can span vehicles and years. Put the actual label next to the number, even if it makes the spreadsheet a little less neat. It will make the funding conversation much less confusing.


## Find an investment the fund made recently


Start with recent investments the firm or the company announced. Look for a first check at the stage you’re raising. A web page can say ‘early stage’ while most visible transactions are later rounds in existing companies. On the other hand, a firm may be active without disclosing every deal. Put ‘unverified’ in the tracker when you don't have evidence. ‘Unverified’ is a reminder to ask, not a reason to tell someone the firm is inactive.


Make the comparison as concrete as you can. An investor who writes a first $500,000 into a pre-product startup may be useful on a $1.5 million first round. A lead who expects to own a substantial share might make sense in a different round. The same fund size can describe completely different behavior. Fit comes down to the particular investor’s check, ownership expectations and reason for being interested.


## Make the announcement earn an action


For each fund, write one sentence explaining why you belong on its list. Then write the question whose answer would make you take it off yours. If someone has publicly backed two companies that sell to your buyer, ask whether those investments reflect a conviction or create a conflict. If the announcement describes a geography or founder requirement, check it before sending anything. A note that passes those tests will have a better opening than ‘congrats on the new fund.’
